masked.business_two_sentences: This company discovers, develops and commercializes antiviral medicines for two major viral diseases, along with a newer cell-therapy oncology business built on an acquisition completed the prior year. Revenue comes mainly from prescription-drug sales through wholesalers and specialty pharmacies, with the newer cell-therapy product contributing a much smaller share so far [g21].

Revenue is earned mainly from prescription-drug sales through wholesalers and specialty pharmacies [g21].

what_changed.fact: Full-year 2018 product sales were $21.7 billion and GAAP diluted EPS was $4.17, while total revenue fell to $22.1 billion from $26.1 billion as HIV growth partly offset a shrinking hepatitis C franchise [g1][g2].
what_changed.relationship_to_business: This is the company's full annual result covering the period through the cutoff, showing the HIV/HCV mix shift central to the business.

what_changed.fact: Full-year HIV product sales rose to $14.6 billion from $13.0 billion behind the 2018 launch of a new single-tablet regimen, while hepatitis C product sales fell to $3.7 billion from $9.1 billion amid competition and fewer new patients [g3][g4].
what_changed.relationship_to_business: Shows the specific franchise-level offset -- one franchise growing, the other shrinking -- driving the FY2018 revenue mix.

what_changed.fact: Management issued full-year 2019 product-sales guidance of $21.3-21.8 billion, built around anticipated U.S. generic competition for two non-antiviral products and the fuller European impact of generic tenofovir products [g7].
what_changed.relationship_to_business: The company's own forward view heading into the horizon period, already pricing in specific anticipated competitive losses.

programs.program: KTE-X19 in relapsed/refractory adult acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL)
programs.drug_mechanism: KTE-X19: an investigational CAR T-cell therapy -- a patient's own immune T-cells are genetically modified outside the body to target the CD19 protein on cancer cells, then infused back into the patient.
programs.ownership: Wholly owned; developed through the company's cell-therapy subsidiary
programs.trial_id: ZUMA-3 (company study name; ClinicalTrials.gov identifier not independently verified before cutoff, see missing_data)
programs.design: Single-arm, uncontrolled (no randomization or comparator arm) study [g10]

sample_size.enrolled: not stated as a specific count in this excerpt
sample_size.analyzed: response assessed among 'evaluable patients' at a median follow-up of 15.1 months

programs.population: Adults with relapsed or refractory acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL), a blood cancer
programs.primary_endpoint: Not detailed in eligible sources beyond the complete-remission and minimal-residual-disease rates reported
programs.latest_evidence: 69% of evaluable patients achieved complete tumor remission after a single infusion; all (100%) of those complete responders had undetectable minimal residual disease (a sensitive measure of remaining leukemia cells), at a median follow-up of 15.1 months [g10]
programs.management_says_vs_regulator: Company-reported update from an uncontrolled early-stage study; no independent regulator statement or peer-reviewed publication is in this packet
programs.economic_relevance: Early-stage pipeline extension of the existing CAR-T cell-therapy platform, which generated $264 million of FY2018 product sales via the approved lymphoma product; no separate revenue yet

programs.drug_mechanism: GS-9674: an investigational, orally administered drug that selectively activates the farnesoid X receptor (FXR), a protein involved in regulating bile-acid levels in the liver.
programs.phase: Early-stage (specific phase not stated in this excerpt)
programs.population: Patients with primary sclerosing cholangitis, a chronic liver disease involving bile-duct inflammation and scarring
programs.latest_evidence: Reported significant improvements in liver biochemistry and markers of cholestasis (impaired bile flow) [g12]
programs.management_says_vs_regulator: Company-reported result; no independent regulator statement or publication is in this packet
programs.economic_relevance: Early-stage program outside the company's core HIV/HCV/oncology commercial franchises; no product sales

programs.program: Two-year follow-up of the approved CAR-T product in refractory large B-cell lymphoma
programs.drug_mechanism: Axicabtagene ciloleucel: the same CD19-directed CAR T-cell therapy approach as the ALL program above, already FDA-approved for this related lymphoma indication.
programs.phase: Approved product; post-marketing long-term follow-up of the pivotal trial
programs.ownership: Wholly owned; approved product generating $264 million of FY2018 sales [g5]
programs.design: Single-arm, uncontrolled pivotal trial as originally conducted; this update covers longer follow-up of the same trial [g11]

catalysts.description: Chief-executive transition: an incoming CEO becomes Chairman and CEO effective March 1, 2019, following an interim CEO who served from January 1 to March 1, 2019 [g8].
Full-year 2019 product-sales guidance of $21.3-21.8 billion, explicitly built around anticipated new U.S. and European generic competition [g7].

unresolved_questions: Whether HIV franchise growth (led by the 2018 launch) can keep outpacing the ongoing hepatitis C decline as anticipated 2019 generic competition affects two other products.
Whether the earlier-stage oncology and liver-disease pipeline can diversify revenue beyond the HIV/HCV franchises before further competitive erosion.
How the incoming CEO transition, effective March 1, 2019, affects capital-allocation priorities such as R&D spending, buybacks and business development.

macro_context.item: Management's 2019 guidance and its own forward-looking risk disclosure both flagged anticipated U.S. and European generic competition -- for two non-antiviral products, for continuing tenofovir disoproxil fumarate erosion in Europe, and for two older antiviral HIV products -- as a headwind [g7][g14].
macro_context.business_connection: This is the structural generic-competition backdrop shaping the company's official 2019 product-sales guidance range.

macro_context.item: The hepatitis C franchise's decline was attributed to lower average selling prices and lower sales volume amid increased competition and fewer new patients starting treatment [g4].
macro_context.business_connection: This is the industry-level dynamic behind why the hepatitis C franchise, once the company's largest, continues shrinking even as the HIV franchise grows.

own: HIV product sales grew to $14.6 billion from $13.0 billion behind the 2018 launch, lifting HIV to about 66% of total revenue from about 50% a year earlier -- evidence the newest franchise addition is more than offsetting the hepatitis C decline [g3][g20].

The company generated $8.4 billion of operating cash flow and held $31.5 billion of combined cash and investments at year-end 2018, even after paying $3.0 billion of dividends, repurchasing $2.9 billion of stock and repaying $6.3 billion of debt during the year [g6].

Two-year follow-up data on the approved cell-therapy product (39% of patients in an ongoing response) and an early signal in a related leukemia study (69% complete remission) suggest the CAR-T franchise, still only $264 million of FY2018 sales, has room to expand within its approved and pipeline indications [g11][g10].
flat: Management's own full-year 2019 product-sales guidance of $21.3-21.8 billion is roughly flat to down versus FY2018's $21.7 billion, explicitly built around anticipated new U.S. and European generic competition [g7].

Total revenue fell to $22.1 billion from $26.1 billion and GAAP operating margin fell to 37.1% from 54.1%, so even with the HIV offset, overall scale and profitability both declined for the year [g2][g16].
short: Hepatitis C product sales fell to $3.7 billion from $9.1 billion in a single year -- a franchise that once anchored the company's growth -- and management's own risk disclosure separately flagged expected erosion from generic versions of two older HIV products [g4][g14].

R&D expense growth included an $820 million impairment on an early-stage, in-licensed multiple-myeloma program, and full-year results absorbed a Q4 2018 unfavorable $0.99-per-share impairment/tax charge tied to the 2017 cell-therapy acquisition -- signs of integration costs still working through results [g19][g18].
